lead: Two barren women, two angels, two sons set apart before their birth. The reading from Judges and the Gospel of Luke are told almost in the same words, and the Church places them side by side on purpose. God begins his great deliverances where human hope has run out. Samson will “begin to deliver” Israel; John will prepare a people for the Lord himself. Psalm 71 is the prayer of one who has relied on God “from my mother's womb”.

r.h: The birth of Samson is announced
set: The Book of Judges tells a repeated story: Israel does evil, falls under an enemy, cries out, and God raises up a deliverer. Chapter 13 opens with Israel forty years under the Philistines (13:1), and this time no cry is recorded. God acts first. The scene is a small home of the tribe of Dan, in Zorah, in the foothills west of Jerusalem.
str: v. 2: Manoah and his barren wife, who is never named.
vv. 3–5: the angel's message: a son, a nazirite, a beginning of deliverance.
vv. 24–25a: the birth, the name, the first stirring of the Spirit.
kw: The same word is used of Sarah, Rebekah and Rachel (Genesis 11:30; 25:21; 29:31). In Israel's story it signals that a child will be God's gift and a turning point in the history of his people.

Numbers 6:1–21 describes a vow by which a man or woman is consecrated to God for a time: no wine, no razor, no touching a dead body. Samson's case is unusual, since the consecration is lifelong and starts before birth, and it binds his mother as well.
God's messenger, in whom God himself is often felt to be present. The woman describes him as “most awe-inspiring” (13:6).
vv: “Although you are barren, having borne no children, you shall conceive and bear a son.
The form of the announcement is a fixed one in Scripture: appearance, promise, name or mission. The same form returns today in Luke, and tomorrow for Mary.
It is he who shall begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines.

Only “begin”. Samson's life, read on in chapters 14 to 16, is a strange mixture of strength and failure, and the Philistines are still there at the end. Israel's real deliverance lies ahead. The Letter to the Hebrews still numbers him among those of faith (Hebrews 11:32).
The woman bore a son, and named him Samson. The boy grew, and the Lord blessed him.
A quiet sentence very like the ones Luke uses of John and of Jesus (Luke 1:80; 2:40).
ch: The Catechism sees in such women the preparation for Mary: against all human expectation God chooses those who were considered powerless and weak to show his faithfulness (CCC 489). Samson is thus a figure in the old sense: he points beyond himself. His consecration from the womb and his partial deliverance prepare us to hear of one who will be greater.

r.h: The birth of John the Baptist is announced
set: After a short preface (1:1–4), Luke begins his Gospel in the temple in Jerusalem, and he will end it there (24:53). “Herod” is Herod the Great, who died about 4 BC. David's arrangement divided the priests into twenty-four orders, each serving in turn; Abijah's was the eighth (1 Chronicles 24:10). There were many priests, so the task of offering incense was given by lot, and later Jewish tradition suggests that a priest might have it only once in his life. So this is the greatest hour of Zechariah's life, and God meets him in it.
str: vv. 5–7: the couple: righteous, childless, old.
vv. 8–10: the hour of incense, with the people praying outside.
vv. 11–17: the angel: your prayer has been heard; a son named John.
vv. 18–20: Zechariah's question and the sign.
vv. 21–25: the people wait, he comes out mute; Elizabeth conceives.
kw: The Hebrew meanings are widely noted: Zechariah, “the Lord has remembered”; Elizabeth, “my God has sworn” or “my God is an oath”; John, “the Lord is gracious”. Put together, they almost tell the story.

Probably “God is my strength” or “mighty one of God”. In Daniel he comes at the time of the evening offering to explain the time of salvation (Daniel 8:16; 9:21). That he appears now tells the reader that the time has come.
the spirit and power of Elijah
Malachi ends the prophets with the promise that Elijah will return and “turn the hearts of parents to their children” (Malachi 4:5–6). The angel quotes that promise.
vv: Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you will name him John.
They may have stopped praying for a child long ago. God has not forgotten. An old prayer can be answered at a time when no one is expecting it.
With the spirit and power of Elijah he will go before him
“Him” here is the Lord God of v. 16. John goes before God. By the end of the story, the one who comes after John is Jesus. Luke is saying something tremendous about who Jesus is, with no fuss at all.
“How will I know that this is so? For I am an old man, and my wife is getting on in years.”
Abraham asked something similar (Genesis 15:8). But the angel takes it as unbelief (v. 20), and the priest who should have blessed the waiting people (Numbers 6:22–27) comes out unable to speak.
“This is what the Lord has done for me when he looked favorably on me and took away the disgrace I have endured among my people.”
Elizabeth, who is given no angel, is the first in this Gospel to praise God for what he has done. Childlessness in her world was felt as a public shame, and she names it, and names its end.
ch: The Catechism says that John was filled with the Holy Spirit “even from his mother's womb” (CCC 717), that he is Elijah who must come (CCC 718) and that he is the Lord's immediate forerunner (CCC 523). The Church keeps his birthday as a solemnity on 24 June, a rare honour: besides the Lord, only Mary and John have their earthly birth kept in the Roman calendar.

qa: Why was Zechariah punished for his question and Mary not for hers?

The words are close, but Luke marks a difference. Zechariah asks for proof, “How will I know?”, and the angel names it unbelief (1:20). Mary asks how it will come about, “How can this be?”, and then gives her consent (1:34, 38). Fathers such as St Ambrose see this difference (in substance). And Zechariah's silence ends in praise: when his tongue is released, his first words are a blessing (1:64).
rite: Today's O Antiphon is O Radix Jesse, “O Root of Jesse”, from Isaiah 11:1, 10. It fits a day of barren women: a root seems dead, and God brings life from it.
study: Is there an old prayer I have stopped praying because it seems too late? What would it mean to bring it back to God this Advent?
Elizabeth gives thanks in hiddenness for five months. Where could I use some quiet in these last days before Christmas, to see what the Lord has done for me?
